Wa l l a c e , Cir c u it  Ju d g e , dissenting:
I respectfully dissent.
I concur in the majority’s interpretation of the Administrative 
Procedure Act and the Federal Water Pollution Control Act Amendments 
of 1972. I respectfully dissent, however, with respect to the majority’s 
disposition of petitioners’ constitutional challenges. * * *
No t e s
1. The Rise (and FalU) of a Deference-Based Approach. Like the Ninth 
Circuit in Marathon Oil, both the D.C. Circuit and the First Circuit at one time 
applied a presumption that a statutory “hearing” requirement in adjudication 
requires a formal hearing conducted under the APA’s hearing provisions. See 
Union of Concerned Scientists v. U.S. NRC, 735 F.2d 1437, 1444 n. 12 
(D.C.Cir.l984); Seacoast Anti-Pollution League v. Costle, 572 F.2d 872, 877 (1st 
Cir. 1978). Both courts discarded the pro-formality presumption following the 
Supreme Cowrt’s decision in Chevron U.S A., Inc. v. NRDC, 467 U.S. 837 
(1984), which required courts to defer to an agency’s reasonable interpretation 
of the statute the agency administers (this doctrine is examined in Chapter 7).
In Chemical WasteMgm't, Inc. v. EPA, 873 F.2d 1477 (D.C. Cir. 1989), the 
D.C. Circuit held that Chevron required it to defer to an agency’s determination 
of whether its organic statute requires an on-the-record “hearing” under the 
APA. The First Circuit followed suit in Dominion Energy Brayton Point, LLC 
V. Johnson, 443 F.3d 12 (1st Cir. 2006) (overriding Seacoast Anti-Pollution 
League). Some scholars raised doubts about this approach. See, e.g., William 
S. Jordan, III, Chevron and Hearing Rights: An Unintended Combination, 61 
Ad min . L. Re v . 249 (2009). As Florida East Coast Railway demonstrates, an 
agency’s statutory obligation to conduct a formal hearing under the APA 
depends on a complex interrelationship between the agency’s organic statute 
and the APA. By focusing on whether the plain language of the agency’s statute 
unambiguously requires a formal hearing, the D.C. Circuit’s approach in 
Chemical Waste effectively removed the APA—and the complexities of 
determining whether the agency’s action has a quasi-judicial or quasi-
legislative character—^from the analysis. In addition, courts generally declined 
to afford Chevron deference to an agency’s interpretation of a statute that it 
has no special responsibility for administering. The APA is a core example. 
See, e.g.. Profl Reactor Operator SoFy v. NRC, 939 F.2d 1047, 1052 (D.C. Cir.
